h1: Why craft beer costs more than mass-market lager
title: Why Craft Beer Costs More | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a craft pint costs more than mass-market lager in India: scale, ingredients, imported hops, batch size, cold chain and state excise explained.
teaser: The gap between a craft pint and a big-brand lager is not all margin. Most of it is malt, hops, scale and a cold truck.
standfirst: People often assume craft brewers simply charge more because they can. The real reasons sit in the recipe, the size of the brewhouse and the journey from tank to glass.
sections:
A large lager brewery may brew more in a day than a brewpub makes in a year. That changes everything. Big plants buy malt in bulk, run automated lines around the clock and spread the cost of every engineer, lab technician and bottling line over enormous volumes.

A craft brewery with a 10 hectolitre brewhouse still pays its brewer a full wage and still needs tanks, chillers and a cleaning regime, but it sells a tiny fraction of the beer. Fixed costs land on far fewer pints. That alone explains much of the difference before a single ingredient is counted.

Many mass-market lagers use a share of rice or maize alongside barley malt. These adjuncts are cheaper sources of fermentable sugar and give a light, crisp beer. They are a legitimate brewing choice, used for good reasons. They also keep the cost of extract low.

Craft recipes usually lean on all-malt grists, often with speciality malts for colour and flavour. A strong stout or a double IPA needs far more grain per litre than a 5% lager, because alcohol comes from sugar and sugar comes from grain. Our guide on what craft beer is covers the wider differences.

Hops are the other big line. A light lager may carry a modest dose. A hazy IPA can use many times that, much of it added after the boil purely for aroma. That hop material soaks up beer that never reaches a glass, so a brewer loses a few per cent of every batch to wet hop sludge at the bottom of the tank.

Yeast is a smaller cost but a real one. Big plants propagate and repitch their own house strain for many generations. A small brewery making six styles may buy fresh yeast for several of them.

India grows almost no aroma hops and little of the speciality malt craft recipes call for. Craft brewers import most of their hops and many of their malts and yeasts from Europe, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. They pay freight, import duty and the swings of the rupee against the dollar and the euro.

Large brewers import too, but they buy at volume, contract ahead and lean on local barley for much of their grist. A small brewery ordering a few hundred kilograms of hops a year has none of that buying power.

Craft beer is usually sold fresh and often unpasteurised. Hop aroma fades within weeks, so a brewery cannot brew a huge batch and let it sit for months. Smaller, more frequent brews mean more cleaning, more labour and more time per litre.

Lagers add another cost: time. A properly lagered beer sits cold in a tank for several weeks, typically at 0 to 2 °C after fermentation. That tank is not making anything else meanwhile. In a small brewery, tank space is the tightest resource of all.

Fresh beer needs to stay cold from tank to glass. In Indian heat that is expensive. Refrigerated storage, chilled transport and cold rooms at outlets all add up. Beer that sits warm for a week loses its hop character and can turn stale, so a brewery that cares about quality pays for the cold.

Then there is tax. Excise and related levies on beer are set state by state in India and they change. They can be a large share of what you pay at the counter. How they are calculated also differs between states. Our explainer on beer excise duty in India walks through how the system works. For current rates, check your state's latest notification.

None of this means every expensive beer is good. Price tells you about cost, not quality. A badly brewed IPA made with costly imported hops is still badly brewed, while a well-made lager from a big plant can be a fine drink.

What a craft price should buy you is freshness, flavour that matches the label and a beer brewed in small enough volumes that someone tasted that batch. The useful skill is telling whether you got it. Can you spot an IPA that has gone stale? A lager with a buttery fault? Once you can, you stop paying for disappointment.
faqs: Is craft beer more expensive because of tax?
Tax is part of it, but it applies to all beer. The bigger differences are scale, ingredients, imported hops and malt, small batches and the cost of keeping fresh beer cold.
Why do rice and maize make lager cheaper?
They are cheaper sources of fermentable sugar than barley malt and give a light, crisp beer. They are a normal brewing choice, not a shortcut to a bad beer.
Does a higher price mean better beer?
No. Price reflects cost. Freshness, clean brewing and good storage decide quality. You can learn to taste the difference.
